translate.output: Then does the meaning of freedom, in fact, not apply to individuals? I say: What absurd words! The freedom of a group is the accumulation of individual freedoms. Humans cannot survive apart from groups; if a group fails to protect its own freedom, another group will invade it from outside, suppress it, and seize it—then what individual freedom remains? A scholar like me, with limited learning, dares to attempt to expound this in mere brief words; how could I possibly know whether it is correct?... Are there those who love freedom? Then beware: do not poison freedom so as to poison the world.
translate.gold: In that case, can freedom after all not be applied to the individual? I answer: nonsense, what talk is this? Collective freedom is the sum of individual freedoms. People cannot survive on their own apart from the group. If the group does not protect its freedom, then other groups will come from outside to invade it, oppress it and plunder it, and then what will be left of the individual's freedom? For one of shallow learning like me to try to explain it in a few paltry words: how can I know that it will do? … Are there people in the world who love freedom? Let them take care not to poison freedom, and thereby poison the world.

translate.output: On the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of Guangxu, the Inner Cabinet received an imperial edict: For several years, officials both within and without China have focused on current affairs, mostly advocating reform for self-strengthening. Recently, several imperial decrees have been issued—for example, establishing a special examination, reducing redundant troops, reforming the military examination system, and founding primary and secondary schools—all of which have been carefully deliberated multiple times, thoroughly planned, and are now just beginning to be implemented. However, public opinion has not yet fully opened; opinions remain divided. Some, claiming to act out of concern for the nation's welfare by citing their experience, insist that old regulations must be strictly followed and new methods must be completely rejected. Many voices clamor with empty words that offer no real benefit. Consider today's situation: if we continue with untrained troops, limited funds, scholars without practical knowledge, and artisans without competent teachers, while strength and weakness contrast sharply and poverty and wealth remain vastly unequal, how can we truly wield a simple stick to strike armored soldiers wielding sharp weapons? ... The Imperial University in the capital serves as a model for all provinces; it should be established first. It is ordered that the Grand Councilors and the Ministers in charge of affairs with foreign countries jointly deliberate promptly and submit a proper report. ... This edict is hereby promulgated to all. So be it.
translate.gold: On the 23rd day of the 4th month of the 24th year of Guangxu, the Grand Secretariat received the following edict: For several years now, officials at court and in the provinces have studied current affairs, and most have advocated reform and self-strengthening. Recently edicts have been issued one after another: setting up a special examination, cutting surplus troops, reforming the military examinations, establishing schools of all levels. All were examined again and again and planned most thoroughly, and it has only just been proposed to put them into effect. But attitudes are not yet open, and opinions cannot agree. Some take cover behind experience and concern for the country, holding that the old institutions must be held fast and the new methods rejected. Many mouths clamour, but empty words are of no help. Let us ask: with the situation as it is today, and the state's strength as it is, if we still rely on untrained troops and limited funds, with scholars lacking practical learning and artisans lacking good teachers, the strong and the weak set side by side, the rich and the poor so far apart, can we really make clubs to beat strong armour and sharp weapons? … The Imperial University in the capital is to be an example to the provinces and above all should be set up first. Let the Grand Councillors and the princes and ministers of the Zongli Yamen deliberate on it jointly and report properly and quickly by memorial. … Let this be proclaimed to all. Respect this.

translate.output: The Minister of the Interior, Cheng Dequan, submits this report. It is understood that protecting the people and safeguarding the nation makes police administration a pivotal mechanism; selecting worthy individuals and appointing capable persons makes schools a reservoir for cultivating talent. Upon examination, Nanjing now serves as the foremost exemplary region; all police matters must be earnestly improved first, so that it may set an example for other provinces. However, since our department was recently established, funding is difficult; therefore, regarding donations, we should strive to exercise strict economy. Accordingly, the former Jiangnan Higher Police Academy has been converted into the Ministry of the Interior's Police School. We have initially recruited 240 police trainees from the training institute, organized them into specialized departments for instruction, as a temporary measure to address urgent needs. As for regular class students, once funds are secured, we will conduct recruitment and provide proper education, thereby fulfilling the Great President's intention of promoting public happiness. We have immediately appointed Sun Runyu, Director of Police Affairs in our department, to concurrently serve as Principal of the Police School, with the aim of expediting its establishment, so that both public and private interests may benefit. Regarding the reasons for opening the Police School, it is appropriate to submit this document for review and implementation. Thus ends the memorial.
translate.gold: Cheng Dequan, Minister of the Interior, reports as follows. I humbly consider that for protecting the people and defending the state, police affairs are the key to administration; and for choosing the worthy and employing the able, schools are the place where talent is gathered. I note that Nanjing is now the capital, and all police matters must first be thoroughly reformed before it can serve as a model for the provinces. But this ministry has only just been founded and funds are difficult, so all measures should, it seems, be as economical as possible. I have therefore converted the existing Jiangnan Higher Police School into the Ministry of the Interior Police School. It will first recruit 240 police cadets for the training institute and teach them by subject, as an emergency measure. As for students of the regular course, as soon as definite funds have been raised, they will be admitted by examination and educated, so as to fulfil the President's intention of working to advance the people's happiness. I have also at once appointed Sun Runyu, head of this ministry's police bureau, as principal of the police school concurrently, in the hope of setting it up quickly, so that both public and private interests may benefit. As to the opening of the police school, it is proper to prepare this document and request you to examine it and put it into effect. This petition is necessary. According to your petition, the land on the west shore of Lake Shaobo has long lain waste, and you representatives cannot bear to leave its profit in the ground and plan to reclaim and cultivate it. This truly cannot be delayed. But you should measure in mu how much land there is on that shore, draw a map and first submit them to the ministry, so that we can pass them on with an order to the civil governor of Yangzhou to verify. You representatives are directed to comply at once, and also to draw up proper regulations and procedures for raising capital, and submit them to the ministry together. This is the ruling.

translate.output: Huxley, alone in a room in southern England, with his back to the mountains and facing the wilds, could see clearly through the lattice outside as if they were right beneath him. He then imagined what scenery existed here two thousand years ago, before the Roman general Cato arrived... Thus we know that the statement 'nothing changes' is certainly not true of natural processes. Rather, the principle by which things endure over long periods lies precisely in constant change. What we see now may transform after twenty or thirty years; it may also transform after two or three ten thousand years. We can infer from past events that change will continue indefinitely, though we do not know its ultimate limit. Nevertheless, although natural processes change, there are unchanging principles operating within them. What remains unchanged? This is called 'natural evolution.' Taking natural evolution as the substance, it has two functions: competition among things and selection by nature. All living things follow this, especially those with life. Competition means things strive to preserve themselves. When one thing competes with others, some survive while others perish, and the outcome returns to selection by nature. Selection by nature means that among competing things, only some survive. For such survival, there must be a reason: it is what nature has allotted, combined with its own capabilities, the time and place it encounters, and all external forces around it, which together conspire and balance each other. Only then can it avoid extinction and stand on its own. From the effect observed, such a thing appears specially favored by nature for selection and survival—this is what we call 'selection by nature.' Selection by nature chooses according to natural laws; though it chooses, nothing seems to be chosen, just as competition appears aimless yet is in fact the utmost struggle. Spencer said: 'Selection by nature preserves that which is most suitable.' Since things already compete for survival, and nature follows this competition to select among them, one act of competition followed by one act of selection brings about change.
translate.gold: Huxley is sitting alone in a room in the south of England, with hills behind and fields in front; the scenes beyond the railing are as clear as if they lay below his desk. He then imagines what this place looked like two thousand years ago, before the Roman general Caesar came. …… Hence we know that "unchanging" is by no means the way of heaven's course, and that the principle by which things endure and take shape lies, on the contrary, in ceaseless change. What we see before us may well be transformed in twenty or thirty years, or again in twenty or thirty thousand. It is only that, inferring the future from past events, change has far still to run, and we do not know where it will end. And yet, though heaven's course changes, something unchanging operates within it. What is this unchanging thing? It is called evolution (天演). Evolution is the substance, and it has two functions: the struggle of things (物競) and the selection of heaven (天擇). This is so of all things, and most evident among living things. The struggle of things is things striving to preserve themselves. When one thing contends with thing after thing, it either survives or perishes, and the result comes down to the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is when things contend and one alone survives. Then there must be a reason for its survival: its endowment from heaven, the abilities it attains by itself, the time and place it meets with, and all the forces of things outside its body must have worked together and complemented one another. Only then does it alone escape perishing and become able to stand on its own. And looking at it from the result, it is as if this thing had been specially favoured by heaven and selected to survive: this is what is called the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is selection by nature: it selects, yet no one selects; just as the struggle of things seems to be no struggle, and is in truth the fiercest struggle in the world. Spencer said: "The selection of heaven is the preservation of the fittest." Since things struggle to survive, and heaven then selects among them after their struggle, with each struggle and each selection, change comes about.

中國政治與文化之變革，莫劇於殷周之際。殷周間之大變革，自其表言之，不過一姓一家之興亡與都邑之移轉；自其裏言之，則舊制度廢而新制度興，舊文化廢而新文化興。又自其表言之，則古聖人之所以取天下及所以守之者，若無以異於後世之帝王；而自其裏言之，則其制度文物與其立制之本意，乃出於萬世治安之大計，其心術與規摹，迥非後世帝王所能夢見也。欲觀周之所以定天下，必自其制度始矣。

周人制度之大異於商者：一曰「立子立嫡之制」，由是而生宗法及喪服之制，並由是而有封建子弟之制、君天子臣諸侯之制；二曰「廟數之制」；三曰「同姓不婚之制」。此數者皆周之所以綱紀天下，其旨則在納上下於道德，而合天子、諸侯、卿大夫、士、庶民以成一道德之團體。周公制作之本意實在於此。此非穿鑿附會之言也。

translate.output: The transformation of Chinese politics and culture was no more profound than at the transition between Yin and Zhou. From an external perspective, the great change between Yin and Zhou involved merely the rise and fall of one family and the relocation of the capital; from an internal perspective, old institutions were abolished and new ones established, old culture discarded and new culture adopted. Externally, the ancient sages' methods for acquiring and maintaining rule appear no different from those of later emperors; internally, however, their institutions, cultural artifacts, and the original intent behind establishing them were designed for universal stability across generations, with moral principles and planning far beyond what later emperors could even conceive. To understand how Zhou stabilized the world, one must begin with its institutions. The major differences between Zhou and Shang systems are: first, the system of appointing sons as heirs based on legitimacy (嫡), which generated the clan system (宗法) and mourning attire regulations (喪服), and from this also arose the feudal system for descendants and the structure of emperor ruling over lords; second, the system of ancestral temple counts; third, the prohibition of marriage within the same surname. These three principles formed the framework by which Zhou governed the world. Their purpose was to integrate all levels of society into moral order, uniting the emperor, lords, ministers, nobles, and commoners into a single moral community. The original intent behind Duke of Zhou's institutional creations lies precisely here. This is not forced or fanciful interpretation; the arguments in this essay are grounded in historical facts, which I will briefly outline. Regarding the rules, the *Zuo Zhuan* (Commentary of Zuo on the Spring and Autumn Annals) states: 'If the crown prince dies, appoint his younger full brother if available; if not, appoint the eldest son. If ages are equal, choose the more capable one; if moral standing is equal, resort to divination.' The *Gongyang* school argues: 'According to ritual, if the principal wife bears no sons, establish the right concubine (right attendant); if she also bears no sons, establish the left concubine...' Between these two interpretations, the latter is more detailed, yet both are later scholars' extrapolations; at the time of initial legislation, such comprehensive variations were likely not fully developed. Nevertheless, the core principle 'appoint a son based on status rather than age, and an heir based on seniority rather than virtue' represents the essence of hereditary succession law. Although this exact phrasing may not have existed then, the underlying intent was already in practice.
translate.gold: Of all the changes in China's government and culture, none is more drastic than that at the transition from Shang to Zhou. …… The great change between Shang and Zhou, seen from the surface, was no more than the rise and fall of one family and the moving of the capital; seen from within, old institutions fell and new institutions arose, old culture fell and new culture arose. Again, seen from the surface, the ways in which the ancient sages won the empire and kept it seem no different from those of later emperors; but seen from within, their institutions, their culture and their original intention in founding the institutions came in fact from a grand plan for order and peace for ten thousand generations, and their thinking and design were far beyond anything later emperors could dream of. If one wishes to see how the Zhou settled the empire, one must begin from its institutions. The Zhou institutions that differ greatly from the Shang are, first, the institution of succession by the son and by the son of the principal wife, from which arose the lineage system and the mourning system, and from which came the enfeoffment of sons and younger brothers and the system in which the Son of Heaven is lord and the feudal lords are subjects; second, the number of ancestral temples; third, the rule that those of the same surname do not marry. These are all the means by which the Zhou gave order to the empire. Their purpose was to bring high and low within morality, and to unite the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords, ministers, great officers, gentlemen and the common people into one moral community. The Duke of Zhou's original intention in making institutions truly lay here. These are not far-fetched or forced words: everything this essay argues has facts as its evidence. Let me set it out briefly. …… The rules are given in the account of the *Zuo Commentary*: "When the heir dies, if there is a younger brother by the same mother, he is made heir; if not, the eldest is made heir. If they are equal in age, the worthiest is chosen; if equal in merit, the matter is divined." The Gongyang school's account says: "By the rites, if the principal wife has no son, the son of the right secondary wife is made heir; if the right secondary wife has no son, the son of the left secondary wife is made heir; ……" Of these two accounts, the latter is especially detailed, but both are the extrapolations of later Confucians; when the rule was first laid down, its makers did not necessarily work out every case in this way. Yet what is called "a son is made heir by rank, not by age; the son of the principal wife is made heir by age, not by worth" is the essence of the rule of succession by sons; though these words may not have been said at the time, the idea was certainly already in use.
translate.judge_note: The translation's rendering of '萬世治安之大計' as 'universal stability across generations' slightly diminishes the scope of the original, which implies a grand design for the long-term peace and prosperity of the entire world, not just a single generation.

translate.output: My younger brother has long been a friend of Mr. Jifang, and through him I have heard of Yuanfang's excellence; I have always wished to meet him for my own satisfaction. Yesterday, while in the capital city, we met by chance, and I found that Elder Brother's talent and bearing surpass even what I had heard. I regret deeply that our meeting came so late; now that we must part after just one night, I also lament how quickly we are to be separated. After our parting, on the fourth day I arrived in Tianjin, and on the tenth day I visited Pingshu. In less than a month, I have already changed two places. Tired from travel and dust, I find myself merely working as a clerk; I pity myself and even laugh at my own situation. Now that my fellow scholars are returning to their hometowns, I am the only one left in the residence; moreover, with the sound of clear bells and red fish, it feels like practicing cultivation in an ancient temple. As the west wind blows and yellow leaves fall, memories of our past together often arise; surely the gift of the two carp will not abandon me. Has your health recovered? With wedding affairs causing much trouble, please take good care of yourself. Sending this with the wind to convey my thoughts; there is much more I wish to express but cannot fully say here. For a long time I have not seen the graceful appearance of green paulownia and bamboo; whenever the moon is bright and the breeze clear, I deeply long for them. Furthermore, I have been puzzled by your prolonged absence from official duty. Recently I received a letter from Mr. Ruan Xihou, learning that you have traveled to the left side of the state, and that planting lotus in Chuqiu has already been going on for more than a day. Green reeds and jade-like treasures are sold everywhere; this is naturally so. Your younger brother's talent and spirit, I fully believed, would be like a solitary crane on Jishan, sufficient to lift the spirits of the rooster flock; who expected that the zither would be broken and the grass on the grave already grown overnight, causing such deep sorrow! My younger brother first stayed as a guest in western Liaoning, then traveled around Tianjin. This spring he again undertook the mission to Pingshu. Year after year, I am pressed by deadlines, still working as a hired hand; this is truly because village women with beautiful brows are hard for the times to appreciate.
translate.gold: I, your younger brother, formerly had the good fortune to make friends with your younger brother, and so heard of your worth as the elder, and longed for the pleasure of meeting you. Yesterday I met you by chance in the provincial capital, and felt that your talent and bearing surpassed even what I had heard. Just as I was regretting that we had not met sooner, we unexpectedly parted after a single night, and now I regret that we were separated so soon. After we parted, I reached Tianjin on the fourth and went to Pingshu on the tenth: in less than a month I have changed place twice. Travel-worn, I do nothing but weed other people's fields; I pity myself, and can also laugh at myself. Just now my colleagues have gone home, and I live alone in the office; add the clear chime and the red wooden fish, and it is just like an old temple for religious practice. With the west wind and the yellow leaves, I often long for you deeply; you will surely not abandon me, but will send me a letter. Have you recovered your health? With the wedding arrangements so many and tiring, please take good care of yourself. I send my thoughts by the wind, and cannot express all I feel. I have long not seen your bearing, like green parasol trees and jade bamboo; whenever the moon is bright and the wind clear, I long for you in spirit. I had wondered why you had not been on duty for so long. Recently I received a letter from Ruan Xihou and learnt that you have travelled to Shandong and have long been serving in a secretariat at Chuqiu. Fine swords and fine jade are sought after everywhere: that is only to be expected. Your younger brother's talent and spirit, I was sure, like Ji Shao, the lone crane, would shine among the flock of chickens. Who could have expected that Boya's zither would be broken, and that the grass on the grave is already a year old? It moves one to sorrow! I, your younger brother, first lived in Liaoxi, then soon moved to Tianjin and its lakes. This spring I have again taken up a post at Pingshu. Year after year I sew for others, still a hired hand: truly because a village girl's fine eyebrows are hard for the age to admire.
translate.judge_note: The translation renders '碧梧翠竹' as 'green paulownia and bamboo,' which loses some of the original's poetic nuance, as 梧 (wú) refers to a paulownia tree, not a green tree in general.
